clauses.reason: The clause ended by its own terms on 1949-05-29. The order forbids any change, except by agreement, in the conditions out of which the dispute arose, from the order's date and for thirty days after the board made its report to the President. The board's report is shown by the dated transmittal letter, April 29, 1949 (the cited end source; submission date, receipt by the President may have been later). Thirty days after April 29, 1949 is May 29, 1949 (1 day remains in April after the 29th, and 29 more fall in May). The end is recorded inclusive of that day, and the exclusive reading (ending when that day begins) is the alternative. The board's own commands (to investigate and to report) were performed when the report was submitted on 1949-04-29, which is not later than the standstill's end. The thirty-day report deadline is not an end. The dossier's other scopes belong to a separate Civil Service Commission notice and are not clauses of this order. Executive Order 12553, signed February 25, 1986, revokes this order by number and is recorded as the later formal disposition; it is not the first end because the order's own term had already ended. No saving provision appears in it.

research_rationale:
Identity. The held Federal Register text of Executive Order 10048, signed by Harry S. Truman at The White House, March 30, 1949, creates an emergency board under section 10 of the Railway Labor Act to investigate the dispute between the Southern Pacific Company (Pacific Lines), a carrier, and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen. Text printed on the same Federal Register pages outside the order is not part of it. Inventory. The order is one block of text with four commands: create a three-member board, bar members from any interest in an employee organization or carrier, require the board to report within thirty days of the order, and forbid any change except by agreement in the conditions out of which the dispute arose from the order's date until thirty days after the board has made its report. I read the whole text; the one-clause inventory covers all of it and no operative sentence lies outside it. End. The last command to end is the no-change command, which by its own terms runs until thirty days after the board made its report. The report date comes from the held NMB report PDF jobs/ptolemy-custody/output/raw/2f4ad2e942d320d9160f1d190737dc448f6f8cc896f44d557e1254769f22a1af.pdf (SHA-256 verified), Presidential Emergency Board report No. 72 (N.M.B. Case A-3016), through a source excerpt of its cover page and transmittal letter. The letter is dated April 29, 1949 and says the board submits its report herewith. I also read the page image of the letter, which shows the date cleanly; the text layer of the excerpt garbles the year or lacks the line, and the cover page in the same excerpt carries the date. Thirty days after April 29, 1949 is May 29, 1949 (1 day remains in April after the 29th, and 29 more fall in May). I record the end as 1949-05-29, inclusive of that day, under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21; the exclusive reading, under which the command ends when that day begins, is the alternative. The letter date is the date of submission; receipt by the President may have been later, and no held source gives a receipt date. Inventory correction: the dossier inventory (four scopes, lead, 3, c and c-3, over characters 1380 to 5363) includes a Civil Service Commission notice about positions in the National Military Establishment that is printed after the order on the same Federal Register page and is a separate document with its own signature and filing line; the order itself is the single block over characters 617 to 2201 of the held text, ending with the sentence that closes the standstill before Harry S. Truman's signature. I replaced the four scopes with one scope over that span. The notice's dated exception of positions until December 31, 1952 is not an operative term of this order. Later events. Executive Order 12553 (signed February 25, 1986, 51 FR 7237, Federal Register of March 3, 1986) lists this order by number in a table of orders revoked together with any amendments to them; it came 36 years after the own-terms end and is recorded as the formal disposition. Searches. The U.S. Code search (release point through 2026-10-09), the eCFR search as of 2026-10-14 and the Office of the Federal Register disposition-note search returned no other instrument affecting this order apart from the events recorded. Savings: none found.

savings.reason: Executive Order 12553, read in full, is one revoking sentence, a table of revoked orders, an editorial note and the date line, with no saving or transition provision. The commands of this order were a one-time board investigation and report and a standstill that expired by its own terms on 1949-05-29; no held source shows any appointment, transfer or right created under it that survived.
